children: New York-based venture-capital firm Primary Venture Partners plans to open an office in San Francisco, a nod to how critical the city has become for AI investors.

Primary co-founder and General Partner Brad Svrluga said the firm aims to complete the expansion next year. Svrluga said Primary launched with the goal to become the go-to seed-stage investor for New York-based startups. While the firm began expanding its geographic focus during the pandemic, the San Francisco office will be its first outside of New York.

Today, roughly a third of Primary's portfolio companies are based in New York, another third in San Francisco and the remaining third elsewhere across the country and globe, Srvluga said. The firm, which announced its $625 million Fund V early this year, has approximately $1.7 billion in assets under management.

Primary plans to have 12 to 15 San Francisco-based employees by the end of next year, Srvluga said, a mix of "exports from New York" and new San Francisco-based hires. The firm currently has a 70-person team in New York.

The Bay Area has long been an important market for venture capitalists. But San Francisco-home to both Anthropic and OpenAI-has taken on new importance during the AI boom. The Bay Area led the country in the second quarter of this year, securing $98.6 billion in deal value across 761 deals, according to data from PitchBook. New York came in second with $11.7 billion invested across 523 deals over the same period.

Svrluga said Primary's coverage rate, which the firm defines as the percentage of institutional seed deals it sees early enough to have an opportunity to invest, is about twice as high in New York as it is in San Francisco. "We're just not satisfied with half as good coverage in the most important tech market in the world as we have in our homebase, which is the second most important market in the world," Srvluga said.
Other VC firms have established or bolstered their San Francisco presence in recent years.

Primary is looking for office space in San Francisco between the Caltrain station at San Francisco's 4th and King streets near Oracle Park, and Jackson Square, a neighborhood just north of the city's Financial District.

As the valuations of venture-backed companies have climbed in recent years, some venture-capital investors have begun looking outside of hubs like the San Francisco Bay Area and New York to find companies at what they consider to be more reasonable valuations. Srvluga, asked about the dynamic, said Primary's mission is to back the best founders building in the most important markets.
He pointed to Etched, a San Jose-based AI hardware startup whose $5.36 million seed round Primary led in 2023.

"I thought Etched was expensive when we did it at the seed," Svrluga said. But at the startup's current valuation-some $21 billion as of earlier this summer-Primary's investment has grown by a factor of 140, he said.
